newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo private savings fall to 0.15 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Yugo private savings fall to 0.15 pct of GDP.

text.p: Yugoslavs' private savings stood at 118.1 million dinars ($20.9 million) at the end of 1996, falling to 0.15 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), an economic institute said on Monday.
"This means that Yugoslavs saved on the average 11.2 dinars ($1.98) in 1996," Slobodan Milosavljevic of the Institute for Market Research (IZIT) told Reuters.
Savings-to-GDP ratio retains its downward trend since 1994 when it stood at 0.18 percent of GDP. In 1995 it inched down to 0.17 percent of GDP, IZIT said in its latest monthly report.
"Low savings result from bad experience in the past and it is vital for the government to do something to boost savings," Milosavljevic said.
Private savings remain exceptionally low with an issue of frozen old hard currency savings still unregulated, the Belgrade-based IZIT said.
Old hard currency savings stood at around 6.5 billion German marks at the end of 1996, the report said.

Apart from modest earnings of around 702 dinars on the average in December and 618 dinars in January with practically no money left to save, savings position of the nation aggravated twice over last seven years.
Early in the 1990s, the government decided to freeze all hard currency deposits, depriving citizens of their cash. In 1993, Yugoslavs lost more money after two giant pyramid schemes collapsed.
Economists praised the decision by Panonska banka to offer depositors gold collateral for new hard currency savings.
Several other banks also made efforts to boost confidence in the banking system by issuing bilingual savings books in cooperation with foreign banks.

Bankers said such savings books would allow their holders to collect money home and abroad, but there is no confirmation yet that any deal has been sealed. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
